Hi Sandra

# you load a file, I created one:
DATAFILE<-c("This is something that I may have liked when I was
young.", "This is something that I would have liked in May or
September.", "This is something that I may not liked while I am
young.", "No match here, control.")
# uh, what does the second line do, esp. when applied to DATAFILE again?

[1] "am" "young." "No" "match" "here," "control."
# ok, this is the main answer: since "may not" is never spelt together
but will always have a space between "may" and "not", it will always
be split up when you use this line
"DATAFILE2<-unlist(strsplit(DATAFILE,"\\W+"))". Thus, your regex can
never find it as "may not":

(matches.in.datafile<-grep("(^may$|^may.not$)",DATAFILE3,ignore.case=T))
[1] 6 22 30
# the "may" in the first sentence, the "may" in the second sentence,
the "may" in the third sentence (followed by not in [31])

# This also means, however, since all may nots will be retrieved when
you find "may", why use an extra search expression?
for(i in matches.in.datafile) {
cat(DATAFILE3[max(0,i-6):max(0,i-1)],

This is something that I may have liked when I was young.
that I would have liked in May or September. This is something that
September. This is something that I may not liked while I am young.

get all "may not"s together ...
